findings.title: The tick contract is built on a return type that does not exist, and the real boundary problem (state ownership) is unaddressed
findings.description:
Lines 76 and 80 say `tick()` "returns NumPy arrays (positions, velocities)" and frame the central decision as a choice of return type. In the code, `tick()` returns `None` and mutates a caller-owned `AgentState` in place (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py:14-21`). The server owns those arrays and writes to them outside the engine:

- **Bounds policy:** `apply_bounds_policy` rewrites positions and velocities after every tick (`src/migratory_server/simulation.py:115-122`).
- **Entity lifecycle:** `EntityManager` reallocates the arrays on spawn with `np.concatenate` and shifts indices on remove (`src/migratory_server/entities.py:160-200`).
- **Readers:** serialization and the sim logger read the arrays directly (`src/migratory_server/clients.py:194`).

Going to GPU therefore inverts ownership: state must live in Quadrants fields, and every server-side writer becomes a GPU↔CPU round trip or must move into the engine. Options (a)/(b)/(c) do not touch this.

The options themselves have further problems:

- **No decision.** "Support all three behind an abstraction, with the choice made per-platform" defers the one decision this document exists to make (line 18) and commits to three code paths.
- **Option (c) has no consumer.** The server turns state into WebSocket bytes on CPU; `np.from_dlpack` is CPU-only and nothing in `pyproject.toml` consumes a GPU DLPack capsule. It only pays off if culling and delta-encoding run on GPU, which no slice proposes and which would put substrate-specific kernels in the server, violating line 32.
- **Option (b) breaks the threading contract.** 300-arch requires work of 1 ms or more off-loop and serializes state access through a single `sim` worker thread. "Server owns the copy" places a blocking GPU sync on the asyncio thread and touches the Quadrants runtime from a second thread.
- **Line 72 concedes the boundary is misplaced.** "Whether position data exits the GPU at all" means culling must happen before readback at 1M+, yet culling is assigned to the server on the CPU side.

Fix: state the contract as it is (in-place mutation of server-owned arrays). Then decide who owns GPU-resident state, where and on which thread upload and readback happen, and where bounds enforcement, spawn/remove and culling live. Pick (a) for Tier 2 and drop (b)/(c) until a measurement demands them.

findings.title: "Quadrants behind the existing `SpatialQuery` and `BulkForce` interfaces" contradicts the full-GPU tick
findings.description:
Lines 30, 82 and 116 promise Quadrants sits behind interfaces "this initiative optimizes but does not change". Lines 68 and 109 require spatial, forces and integration to all run on GPU. Both cannot hold.

- `BulkForce.__call__` takes a NumPy `AgentState` and `CSRNeighborData` and returns an `N×2` float64 ndarray per force (`src/migratory/engine/forces.py:43-51`).
- `SpatialQuery` returns NumPy `(flat_neighbors, counts)`.
- `tick()` does `exclude_self`, `cumsum`, `concatenate` and force summation in NumPy between those calls (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py:71-104`).

A GPU kernel behind `BulkForce` reads back to host on every force call. The real seam is a whole-tick backend, not per-force and per-query plugs, so the per-force coexistence that works for Numba does not extend to Quadrants.

Line 44's "same CSR-walk pattern" is also questionable on GPU. With `max_neighbors` capping every row, a fixed `(n, k)` buffer is the natural layout; variable-length CSR needs an extra prefix-sum pass for no benefit. The document should also say how the subset-evaluable `active_indices` contract from 100-arch carries over.

findings.title: The fidelity goal has no achievable equivalence criterion (float64 engine vs float32 Metal, chaotic dynamics)
findings.description:
Line 26 requires every tier to be "verifiable against the current NumPy implementation". The engine is float64 throughout (`src/migratory/engine/state.py:16-18`). Metal has no double-precision type, so the Tier 2 backend that line 28 makes first-class runs in float32. Flocking is chaotic, so f32 and f64 trajectories diverge within tens of ticks.

The CPU path has a smaller version of the same problem: Numba explicit loops sum in a different order than `np.add.reduceat`, and any `parallel` or `fastmath` setting widens the gap.

The document never says what "verifiable" means. Candidates are single-tick force-level tolerance from identical inputs, or statistical order parameters over long runs. Line 86 accepts statistical equivalence for staggering only. Without a defined criterion, "mandatory regression testing at each tier transition" cannot be written as a test.

Two related conflicts are not acknowledged:

- **Replay and determinism.** 100-arch's "tick determinism" goal and 300-arch's replay model (initial state plus inputs reconstructs the run) do not survive a cross-backend or cross-GPU change.
- **Engine statefulness.** The `NeighborCache` behind line 86 makes the engine stateful between ticks, contradicting 100-arch ("the engine is stateless between ticks"). Cached neighbor indices also go silently wrong when `remove_entity` shifts indices (`src/migratory_server/entities.py:187-200`).

findings.title: The Tier 1 target (10k at 60 TPS) is not supported by the document's own numbers
findings.description:
Lines 50-56 present "57 TPS at N=3,500" alongside a per-phase budget measured at N=2492 on a synthetic bench. That budget sums to 9.43 ms, a 106 TPS ceiling. The journal's live figures at similar N are about 59 TPS (N=2492) and 79 TPS (N=2500), so 3-7.5 ms of live tick time sits outside the listed phases. The document does not account for it, despite the principle at line 38.

Projecting to 10k with linear scaling (optimistic for the O(n log n) tree), the slice-118 midpoint of 4× on forces, and a 3× stagger on query:

| Phase | Projected ms at 10k |
|---|---|
| build | 1.4 |
| query | 7.6 |
| CSR assembly | 0.8 |
| forces | 3.1 |
| integrate | 0.2 |
| **Total (synthetic)** | **≈13.2** |

Applying the observed live-to-synthetic ratio of 1.3-1.8× gives 17.7-23.7 ms, or 42-56 TPS — below 60. The 2492→59 versus 2500→79 discrepancy also undermines line 58's "roughly linear" conclusion drawn from three points.

Staggering does not reduce tree build: the index is rebuilt over the full population every tick (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py:40`). Line 42's "O(n/k) spatial work" overstates the gain.

findings.title: The wire baseline is factually wrong, and the compression arithmetic is off by an order of magnitude
findings.description:
Line 60 says the protocol is "uncompressed JSON over WebSocket" at 24 bytes per agent. The code is already binary: `[u8 | u32 | u32 | positions_f64 | velocities_f64]`, `9 + N × 32` bytes (`src/migratory_server/protocol.py:174-187`). Consequences:

- **Tier 2's "Binary WebSocket replaces JSON" (lines 68, 101) is a no-op deliverable.**
- **The stated sizes are low.** Actual is 112 KB/tick at 3,500 (not 84) and 320 KB/tick at 10k (not 240). At 60 Hz that is about 154 Mbit/s per client at 10k.
- **"Still viable" for Tier 1 on the current protocol holds only for one loopback client.** 300-arch's stretch NFR (10k × 60 Hz × 20 clients) would be about 3 Gbit/s.
- **Line 88's "~32× compression over float32" is wrong.** int16 against float32 is 2×. Against the real baseline it is 8× (positions only) or 4× (with velocities).

The Tier 2-3 bandwidth claims need recomputing from correct numbers. The cheapest real win, float32 on the wire and dropping velocities, is not listed at all.

findings.title: Wire slices duplicate and conflict with existing slices 319/311, and the delta × culling × decimation × drop interaction is undesigned
findings.description:
`300-slices.worldserver-foundation.md` already defines (319) STATE_UPDATE Delta Encoding and (311) Client Spatial Culling. Lines 101-103 list equivalents as new slices without referencing either, and with a weaker design.

- **No resync.** Line 88 has the client "accumulating deltas onto its last-known positions" with no keyframe. The shipped backpressure policy drops the oldest queued STATE_UPDATE (`src/migratory_server/clients.py:146-151`), and 300-arch accepts up to 5% drops. One dropped delta corrupts the client permanently. Slice 319 has keyframes; this document does not.
- **Per-client streams.** Slice 319 explicitly excludes "per-client delta streams diverging from a shared canonical state". Culling (line 90) and per-client decimation require exactly that: per-client baselines, O(N) server memory per client and per-client encoding. `broadcast()` currently serializes once for everyone (`src/migratory_server/clients.py:194`).
- **No stable identity.** The wire is positional (index i is agent i). A culled, changing visible set needs per-agent IDs or a bitmask, which adds 4 bytes per agent and erases much of the int16 gain. Agents entering the frustum need full positions; the document handles only teleport and spawn.
- **Drift.** Deltas quantized from float accumulate error unless computed against the client's reconstructed position. This is not stated.
- **Reverse channel.** The camera channel breaks 300-arch's "state flows outward" principle; the document should say that principle is being amended.

Line 46 says wire work must not be gated on compute. The tier definitions (lines 66-70) gate it anyway by pinning Tier 1 to the current protocol.

findings.title: The GPU spatial hash, the hardest part, is justified by a misdiagnosis, and the evaluation slice tests the easy part
findings.description:
Line 84 attributes the NumPy hash grid's failure to "bookkeeping overhead" and Python dispatch. Journal Entry 8 gives a different, structural reason for the KD-tree win: the grid "emits all candidates in high-density cells" (185k+ edges versus about 35k), while `cKDTree.query(k)` prunes regardless of density. That candidate blow-up does not go away on GPU.

The engine's semantics are k-nearest within radius (k=13), with per-profile radii. A GPU cell-gather must do per-agent top-k over an unbounded candidate set in dense cells. The Tier 5 demo, two 1M populations colliding around the camera, is by construction the worst dense regime. The document gives no cell sizing, no per-cell cap, and no top-k strategy.

It also assumes parallel radix sort and prefix sum exist as single-kernel primitives. Their availability in Quadrants on Metal is not established here.

The evaluation slice (line 106) benchmarks "a single force", the lowest-risk component. Go/no-go for the substrate should rest on a spatial KNN kernel on Metal in a clustered formation, plus readback cost and f32 behavior.

Line 82's mitigation ("Numba tier provides a working fallback at 10k") is not a mitigation for a 2M goal. No alternative GPU substrate or exit criterion is named.

findings.title: Tiers 3-5 rest on an unvalidated visibility assumption and ignore the project's established multi-resolution strategy
findings.description:
"~50k visible at ground level" (line 70) is unsourced. Frustum culling without a distance or relevance bound does not cap the visible set: a camera inside a 2M-agent collision (line 74) can have a large fraction of the population in its frustum.

300-arch and slice 311 already prescribe the bound: aggregate descriptors for distant groups, a relevance horizon, variable-rate ticking. This document never mentions aggregation or level of detail and brute-forces full resolution to 2M.

Tier 4's alternative, "server-side render path (Vulkan framebuffer → H.264 stream)", contradicts the scope exclusion at line 20 and 300-arch's rule that the server does not own rendering. It has no slice, and it would make the Three.js client and the whole wire track moot.

The gating component for Tiers 4-5 is a browser client ingesting and rendering 1M+ instances over WebSocket. It is declared out of scope while the design goal at line 34 requires a demonstrable artifact at every tier.

findings.title: Overweight: three permanent force backends, three return-type modes, and two undesigned top tiers
findings.description:
"Numba forces coexist with NumPy forces" (line 30) plus "port all BulkForce implementations to `@ti.kernel`" (line 108) means three implementations of every force with no retirement plan. Line 55 says four forces and slice 118 lists five; the engine also ships propulsion, predator-prey and repulsor modules. Initiative 100 still has slices 104 and 115 pending, so each new force would be written three times.

What to cut or defer:

- **NumPy forces:** demote to a test oracle once Numba parity is shown. Numba becomes the only CPU path.
- **Return-type options (b) and (c):** drop them and the "abstraction" over them (line 80) until a measured PCIe cost justifies them.
- **Tiers 4-5:** reduce to a non-binding roadmap paragraph. They contribute no design here (25G LAN, H.264) yet are presented as part of the envisioned state.
- **Cross-platform benchmark harness (line 110):** fold it into the evaluation slice rather than making it a standing deliverable.
- **Biome shading (line 92):** viewer-only and explicitly out of scope by line 20. It does not belong in this document's technical considerations.

findings.title: Scope overlaps initiative 620 and 300's future work, and GPU-resident state may foreclose 300-arch's process-separation path
findings.description:
The initiative plan assigns "GPU-accelerated force accumulation (CuPy/CUDA) and multi-resolution simulation strategies" to initiative 620. `300-slices` Future Work item 2 is "GPU-Accelerated Spatial Queries (WebGPU or CuPy)". This document claims the same ground with a different substrate and neither supersedes nor references them. Related Work (lines 114-118) omits 620, slices 311 and 319, and the initiative plan.

300-arch states the next inflection is "a separate simulation process with shared-memory IPC" and that no v1 decision may preclude it. Quadrants fields and DLPack capsules do not cross a process boundary. The document should say whether the GPU tier is that separate process, or how the two compose.

The frontmatter lists `relatedSlices: [118, 119]` but no `dependsOn`, although the initiative plan declares dependencies on [100, 300].

findings.title: Stack-integration specifics for Numba and Quadrants are missing
findings.description:
Concrete gaps against the project settings:

- **Dependencies.** `pyproject.toml` has `numpy>=1.26` unbounded and `scipy>=1.11`. Numba caps the supported NumPy version per release, so adding it introduces an upper pin. Whether Numba and Quadrants are required or optional extras (as `terrain-lz4` is) is not stated, and line 28 implies they must not be hard requirements.
- **Type checking.** Pyright runs in `strict` mode; untyped `@njit` and kernel decorators trip `reportUntypedFunctionDecorator` and erase signatures. A typing policy is needed.
- **Cold start.** JIT compilation on the first tick is seconds for Numba and more for GPU kernels. That blows the tick budget and the `tests/load/` NFR tests unless caching or warm-up is specified.
- **Threads.** All kernel calls must come from the single `sim` executor thread. Where runtime init happens and which thread does readback is unspecified (see the FAIL finding).
- **CI.** Regression at each tier is "mandatory" (line 26), but CI cannot run Metal or CUDA. The document does not say where GPU parity tests run.
- **API name.** Line 44 writes `@ti.kernel` "(Quadrants)". Confirm the fork's actual import and decorator namespace before slices copy it.

findings.title: Staggered updates are filed as an algorithmic win, but the complexity is unchanged
findings.description: Staggering divides query work by a constant period (default 3 in slice 119) and leaves the build untouched. By the document's own taxonomy that is a constant-factor win. The ordering argument "stagger before Numba" should rest on measurement, and slice 119 in fact depends on 118.
